title: Conceptual Art
objective: After this level you can explain art where the idea matters more than the object.
summary: In conceptual art the idea matters most. LeWitt's wall drawings are instructions others carry out; Kosuth shows one chair as an object, a photo and a definition.

cards.headline: In 2008, a museum filled its walls with new drawings by the late Sol LeWitt.
cards.body: He had died the year before. A team of assistants, students and local artists drew them over nearly six months. Nobody was faking anything. For LeWitt, the drawing on the wall was never the real artwork.

cards.headline: The idea is the machine
cards.body: Conceptual art is art in which the idea matters more than the finished object; it took off in the 1960s. In 1967 LeWitt wrote that the idea is the most important part of the work: "the idea becomes a machine that makes the art." His wall drawings are instructions, often with a diagram. Assistants carry them out on the wall, so each version comes out slightly different, like two cooks following the same recipe.

cards.context: Joseph Kosuth's One and Three Chairs (1965) puts a real wooden folding chair next to a photograph of a chair and an enlarged dictionary definition of the word chair. Kosuth didn't make the chair, take the photo or write the definition; he chose and arranged them. Each is a different kind of chair: a thing you can sit on, a picture of one, and a set of words. So which one is the chair? The object, the picture or the idea? Where the art lives is the question.

mascot.line: You can sit on only one of them. Philosophers are still arguing about the other two.

cards.headline: Conceptual art: thought through
learned: Conceptual art: the idea matters more than the object
LeWitt: "the idea becomes a machine that makes the art"
His wall drawings are instructions others carry out

questions.prompt: Who usually draws a Sol LeWitt wall drawing onto the wall?

options.label: LeWitt himself, freehand and alone
options.rationale: His drawings are carried out by others.

questions.explanation: LeWitt's wall drawings are instructions, often with a diagram, that assistants carry out on the wall.

questions.prompt: Why could new LeWitt drawings be made after he died?

options.label: He left thousands of finished drawings in storage
options.rationale: They were drawn fresh on the walls.

options.label: The museum copied them from photographs
Any artist may sign his name to a wall
options.rationale: They follow his instructions, not their own ideas.

options.label: The idea, his instructions, is the artwork

questions.explanation: For LeWitt the idea is the most important part: the idea becomes a machine that makes the art, so others can carry it out.

questions.prompt: Level 2's customs officers judged sculpture by likeness to nature. Which part of One and Three Chairs looks least like a chair?

options.label: The photograph of the chair
options.rationale: A photo looks exactly like its subject.

options.label: They all look equally like chairs
options.rationale: One of them is only words.

questions.explanation: The definition is just words: no likeness at all. Kosuth's point is that it's still a way of showing a chair.
